questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a hyperlink?
options: <link>
<href>
<url>
questions.explanation: The anchor element <a> with an href attribute creates a hyperlink; <link> sits in the <head> and references external resources such as stylesheets.

questions.question: Which CSS property changes the text color?
options: font-color
text-color
color
foreground
questions.explanation: The color property sets an element's text (foreground) color; font-color and text-color are not valid CSS properties.

questions.question: Which keyword can be used to declare a variable whose value can be reassigned?
options: const
final
let
static
questions.explanation: let declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned; const forbids reassignment, final is Java, and static only marks class members in JavaScript.

questions.question: Which method adds an element to the end of an array?
options: push()
add()
append()
insertEnd()
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.push() appends one or more elements to the end of an array and returns the new length; arrays have no add(), append() or insertEnd() method (append() belongs to Python lists and DOM elements).

questions.question: Which HTTP method is generally used to retrieve data from a server?
options: POST
DELETE
GET
PATCH
questions.explanation: GET retrieves a representation of a resource without changing server state; POST creates, PATCH partially updates and DELETE removes resources.

questions.question: What is React primarily used for?
options: Building user interfaces from reusable components
Handling HTTP routing and middleware on a Node.js server
Querying and managing relational databases
Bundling and minifying JavaScript files
questions.explanation: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of reusable components; server routing, databases and bundling are handled by other tools (Express, SQL engines, Vite/webpack).

questions.question: What is a component in React?
options: A stylesheet scoped to a single page
A global store that holds all application state
A reusable piece of UI that returns JSX
A browser API for sending HTTP requests
questions.explanation: A React component is a reusable function (or class) that takes props and returns JSX describing part of the UI; a global state store is something like Redux or Context.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a REST API?
options: Render HTML on the server before sending it to the browser
Let clients and servers exchange resources over HTTP using standard methods
Keep a persistent two-way socket open between browser and server
Store application data in tables linked by relationships
questions.explanation: A REST API exposes resources (e.g. /users/42) that clients read and change with standard HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE; a persistent two-way socket describes WebSockets.

questions.question: Which SQL command is used to retrieve data?
options: GET
READ
RETRIEVE
SELECT
questions.explanation: SELECT retrieves rows from one or more tables; GET is an HTTP method, and READ/RETRIEVE are not SQL commands.

questions.question: In SQL, what is the purpose of a JOIN?
options: Stack the results of two queries vertically into one result set
Combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column
Group rows that share a value so aggregates can be computed
Copy rows from one table into another table
questions.explanation: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables using a related column (e.g. orders.user_id = users.id); stacking two result sets vertically is UNION, and grouping for aggregates is GROUP BY.

questions.question: What is the purpose of authentication?
options: Verify the identity of a user
Decide which resources a user is allowed to access
Encrypt data while it travels over the network
Record user actions for later auditing
questions.explanation: Authentication answers 'who are you?' by verifying identity (password, OTP, OAuth login); deciding what the user may access is authorization.

questions.question: A logged-in user whose role is 'student' sends DELETE /api/jobs/42 with a valid token, but only admins may delete job posts. Which status code should the API return?
options: 401 Unauthorized
400 Bad Request
405 Method Not Allowed
403 Forbidden
questions.explanation: The user is authenticated but not authorized for this action, which is exactly what 403 Forbidden means; 401 Unauthorized is for missing or invalid credentials, and 405 would mean the resource does not support DELETE at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is commonly used to build a backend REST API?
options: Tailwind CSS
Redux Toolkit
React Testing Library
Node.js with Express
questions.explanation: Express is a minimal Node.js web framework for routes and middleware, a common choice for REST APIs; Tailwind CSS, Redux Toolkit and React Testing Library are frontend styling, state and testing tools.

questions.question: What is database normalization primarily used for?
options: Reducing redundant data and update anomalies
Speeding up every read query by automatically adding indexes to all foreign key columns
Converting all columns to the same data type
Merging related data into one wide table to avoid joins
questions.explanation: Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) organizes tables around keys and dependencies so each fact is stored once, reducing redundancy and update anomalies; merging into one wide table is denormalization.

questions.question: A user submits a registration form. Which sequence best describes the typical flow from the frontend to the database and back?
options: Frontend → Database → Validation/Business Logic → API/Backend → Response → Frontend
Frontend → Validation/Business Logic → Database → API/Backend → Response → Frontend
Frontend → API/Backend → Validation/Business Logic → Database → Response → Frontend
Frontend → API/Backend → Database → Response → Validation/Business Logic → Frontend
questions.explanation: The browser sends the form to an API endpoint; the backend validates input and applies business logic (e.g. hashing the password) before writing to the database, then returns a response. Browsers never talk to the database directly, and validation must happen before the write.

questions.question: Which semantic HTML element is intended for a section containing major navigation links?
options: <span>
<section>
<nav>
<strong>
questions.explanation: <nav> marks a block of major navigation links, which helps screen readers and search engines; <section> is a generic thematic grouping.

questions.question: Which CSS declaration turns an element into a flex container?
options: display: flex;
position: flex;
layout: flex;
flex: display;
questions.explanation: display: flex makes the element a flex container whose direct children become flex items; position and layout do not accept a flex value.

questions.question: What does the JavaScript === operator do?
options: Assigns a value to a variable
Compares only object references in every case
Converts both values to strings before comparison
Compares values without type coercion
questions.explanation: === is strict equality: it compares without converting types, so 1 === '1' is false while 1 == '1' is true.

questions.question: What is JSON commonly used for in web applications?
options: Styling webpages
Exchanging structured data between systems
Compiling JavaScript into native machine code for the browser
Managing operating-system processes
questions.explanation: JSON is a lightweight text format for exchanging structured data, for example between a browser and an API; JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert between objects and JSON text.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code most commonly indicates that a new resource was successfully created?
questions.explanation: 201 Created means the request succeeded and a new resource was created (often with a Location header); 200 is a generic success and 204 means success with no response body.

questions.question: What is React's useEffect hook primarily used for?
options: Memoizing an expensive calculation between renders
Running side effects such as data fetching or subscriptions
Storing a mutable value that does not trigger re-renders
Sharing state with deeply nested components
questions.explanation: useEffect runs side effects such as fetching data, subscriptions or timers after React commits a render; useMemo memoizes calculations, useRef holds mutable values and Context shares state.

questions.question: In React, what is a controlled form input?
options: An input whose value is read from the DOM through a ref only when the form is submitted
An input that has the disabled attribute set
An input rendered only on the server
An input whose value comes from React state and is updated via onChange
questions.explanation: A controlled input takes its value from React state and updates that state in onChange, so React is the single source of truth; reading the value from the DOM through a ref describes an uncontrolled input.

questions.question: What is CORS mainly concerned with in browser-based web applications?
options: Compressing API responses before they reach the browser
Encrypting traffic between the browser and the server so it cannot be read in transit
Blocking every request that does not carry a valid JWT
Controlling whether browser scripts may read responses from a different origin
questions.explanation: CORS lets a server use headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin to tell the browser which other origins may read its responses; it is enforced by browsers and is neither encryption nor authentication.

questions.question: Which statement about a database index is generally correct?
options: It guarantees that every query on the table becomes faster, including writes
It removes the need for primary keys
It can speed up reads but adds storage and can increase write cost
It automatically normalizes every table
questions.explanation: Indexes (usually B-trees) speed up lookups on the indexed columns, but they use extra storage and must be updated on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, so they do not make every query faster.

questions.question: Which technique is a primary defense against SQL injection when accepting user input?
options: Escaping single quotes with a regex before building the query string
Using parameterized queries/prepared statements
Hiding the database port behind a firewall so attackers cannot reach it
Limiting the input length on the frontend form
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries send the SQL and the user input separately, so input is always treated as data and never executed; hand-written escaping is easy to get wrong and frontend checks can be bypassed.

questions.question: A money transfer runs two UPDATE statements in one transaction: debit account A by 500, then credit account B by 500. The database server crashes after the first UPDATE, before COMMIT. After the restart, account A still has its original balance. Which ACID property guarantees this?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
questions.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction's statements take effect together or not at all, so the uncommitted debit is rolled back during recovery; durability only promises that changes which were already committed survive a crash.

questions.question: GET /api/posts returns 50 posts with each author's name. The logs show one query for the posts, followed by 50 separate SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? queries. What is the best fix?
options: Add an index on posts.created_at so the first query runs faster
Raise the connection pool size so the 50 user queries run in parallel
Let the browser fetch each author from /api/users/:id after the posts load
Load all the authors in one go with a JOIN or a single IN (...) query
questions.explanation: This is the N+1 query problem: one query for the list plus one more per item. Loading the authors with a JOIN, eager loading or one WHERE id IN (...) query cuts 51 round trips to one or two, while a bigger pool or client-side fetching still makes 50 extra requests.

questions.question: What does a valid digital signature on a JWT primarily provide?
options: Confidentiality, because the signed payload is encrypted and unreadable by the client
Integrity and authenticity of the token's contents, assuming the key is trusted
Protection against the token being stolen and replayed
Automatic revocation of the token when the user logs out
questions.explanation: A JWT signature lets the server detect tampering and confirm who issued the token, but the payload is only Base64URL-encoded (readable by anyone), and a stolen token stays usable until it expires.

questions.question: Which practice is most directly effective at reducing cross-site scripting (XSS) risk when displaying untrusted content?
options: Store the content in an encrypted database column
Serve every page over HTTPS with a valid TLS certificate and an HSTS header enabled
Apply context-appropriate output encoding/sanitization and avoid inserting raw HTML
Rate-limit the endpoint that saves the content
questions.explanation: XSS happens when untrusted input is rendered as executable HTML/JS, so the direct defence is encoding or sanitizing output for its context (and avoiding innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML with raw input); HTTPS and encryption at rest do not stop injected scripts.

questions.question: Why is an idempotency key useful for a payment-creation API?
options: It encrypts the payment amount so it cannot be tampered with in transit
It lets the client skip authentication when retrying
It lets the server recognise a retried request and avoid creating a duplicate payment
It guarantees requests are processed in the order they were sent
questions.explanation: The server stores the outcome of the first request for each idempotency key and returns it for retries, so a timeout followed by a retry does not charge the customer twice.

options: red
green
black (the browser default)
blue
questions.explanation: An ID selector (1,0,0) is more specific than a class (0,1,0) or a type selector (0,0,1), so blue wins; source order only breaks ties between equally specific rules.

questions.question: An element has width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid black; and the default box-sizing (content-box). How wide is it on screen, excluding margins?
options: 200px
240px
225px
250px
questions.explanation: With content-box, width sets only the content area, so the rendered width is 200 + 2×20 (padding) + 2×5 (border) = 250px; box-sizing: border-box would keep it at 200px.

questions.question: In a flex container with the default flex-direction: row, which declaration on the container centers its items vertically?
options: align-items: center;
justify-content: center;
text-align: center;
vertical-align: middle;
questions.explanation: align-items aligns flex items along the cross axis, which is vertical for a row container; justify-content works along the main (horizontal) axis.

questions.question: Using a mobile-first approach, which media query adds styles only when the viewport is at least 768px wide?
options: @media (max-width: 768px) { ... }
@media (min-width: 768px) { ... }
@media (width: 768px) { ... }
@media (orientation: landscape) { ... }
questions.explanation: Mobile-first CSS writes base styles for small screens and layers larger-screen styles on top with min-width queries; max-width targets screens up to 768px, the opposite direction.

questions.question: A child element has position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0;. Its parent has no position set, but its grandparent has position: relative. Where is the child placed?
options: At the top-right corner of its parent
At the top-right of the viewport, staying fixed while scrolling
At the top-right corner of its grandparent
In normal flow, because top and right are ignored
questions.explanation: An absolutely positioned element is placed relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (position other than static); the parent is static, so the grandparent is the containing block. Staying fixed while scrolling is position: fixed.

questions.question: What does grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); do on a grid container?
options: Fits as many columns of at least 200px as possible and stretches them to fill leftover space
Creates fixed 200px columns that overflow on narrow screens
Creates exactly one column for every child element, no matter how wide the container is
Creates 200 equal columns, each 1fr wide
questions.explanation: auto-fit creates as many tracks as fit the container, and minmax(200px, 1fr) keeps each at least 200px while letting them grow to share free space, giving a responsive grid without media queries.

questions.question:
A submit control is built as
Submit
. Keyboard users cannot reach or activate it, and screen readers do not announce it as a button. Which single change fixes all of these problems?
options: Add role="button" so assistive technology treats the div as a button
Replace the div with a native <button type="submit"> element
Add tabindex="0" so the div can receive keyboard focus
Add aria-label="Submit button" so screen readers read its purpose
questions.explanation: A native <button> is focusable, activates with Enter and Space, exposes the button role and submits its form; role="button" only changes what is announced and tabindex="0" only adds focus, so the div would still need key handlers.

options: Logs 1, then 2
Logs undefined, then undefined
Logs undefined, then throws a ReferenceError
Throws a ReferenceError on the very first line
questions.explanation: var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined, so the first log prints undefined; let is hoisted but stays in the temporal dead zone until its declaration runs, so reading b throws a ReferenceError.

questions.question: A <ul> holds hundreds of <li> items that are added and removed dynamically. What is the most efficient way to handle clicks on any item?
options: Attach one listener to the parent <ul> and use event.target to find the clicked <li>
Attach a separate click listener to every <li> each time the list changes
Use setInterval to check which item currently has focus
Add an inline onclick string attribute to each <li> as it is created
questions.explanation: Click events bubble from the <li> up to the <ul>, so one delegated listener on the parent handles current and future items (event.target.closest('li') finds the item); per-item listeners cost memory and must be re-attached.

undefined
A SyntaxError, because async functions cannot return values
questions.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise, so the log shows a Promise object fulfilled with 42; you need await getScore() or getScore().then(...) to get the number itself.

A D C B
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, D); then the microtask queue (promise callbacks, C) is emptied before the next macrotask (the setTimeout callback, B), even with a 0 ms delay.

questions.explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the same i, which is already 3 when the timers fire; declaring the loop variable with let creates a new binding per iteration and logs 0 1 2.

Meera 2
Ravi 1
Meera 1
questions.explanation: Spread makes a shallow copy: b gets its own name property, but b.skills points to the same array as a.skills, so the push is visible through a. Use structuredClone for a deep copy.

questions.question: A dashboard calls three independent APIs and should show whatever data arrives, even if one call fails. Which approach fits best?
options: await Promise.race([...]) and use whichever settles first
await Promise.all([...]), which resolves with every result even if one request rejects
await Promise.allSettled([...]) and render the fulfilled results
Wrap each fetch in setTimeout so failures do not block the others
questions.explanation: Promise.allSettled waits for every promise and reports each as fulfilled or rejected, so partial data can still be shown; Promise.all rejects as soon as any one promise rejects.

questions.question: Why does React ask for a key prop on items rendered with map()?
options: Keys are required by the browser before it can render <li> elements inside a <ul>
Keys expose the list items to screen readers
Keys act as CSS selectors for styling individual items
Keys let React match items between renders to update, move or remove the right ones
questions.explanation: Keys give each item a stable identity, so reconciliation can tell which items were added, removed or moved and keep the right DOM nodes and state; the browser never sees them.

questions.explanation: Both calls read count from the same render (0), so both schedule the value 1; use the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) when the next state depends on the previous one.

questions.question: Several deeply nested components need the logged-in user's details. Which built-in React feature avoids passing a user prop through every intermediate component?
options: Refs (useRef)
Fragments (React.Fragment)
Context (createContext + useContext)
Portals (createPortal from react-dom)
questions.explanation: Context lets a provider make a value available to any descendant that calls useContext, avoiding prop drilling; refs hold mutable values or DOM nodes, and portals render children into a different DOM node.

questions.question: With React Router, a route is defined as path="/jobs/:jobId". Which hook reads jobId inside the matched component?
options: useParams()
useLocation()
useNavigate()
useSearchParams()
questions.explanation: useParams returns the dynamic segments of the matched URL, e.g. { jobId: '42' }; useSearchParams reads the query string (?page=2) and useNavigate changes routes in code.

questions.question: A profile page fetches /api/users/:id inside useEffect with [id] as the dependency. When the user switches profiles quickly, an older response sometimes overwrites the newer one. What is the best fix?
options: Remove the dependency array so the effect runs after every render
Return a cleanup that aborts or ignores the outdated request
Wrap the fetch call in setTimeout to give earlier requests time to finish
Move the fetch into the component body so it runs during rendering
questions.explanation: React runs an effect's cleanup before re-running it for a new id, so aborting the old request or setting an 'ignore' flag there stops stale responses from updating state; delays and extra renders only hide the race.

options: setInterval cannot be used inside useEffect
clearInterval runs right after the first tick because the cleanup fires on every render
The callback captured count = 0; use setCount(c => c + 1)
State setters cannot be called from asynchronous callbacks
questions.explanation: With an empty dependency array the effect runs once, so the interval callback keeps the count from the first render (0) and sets 1 every second; the updater form always reads the latest state.

questions.question: A parent renders <Row onSelect={() => select(id)} /> where Row is wrapped in React.memo, yet Row re-renders every time the parent renders. Why?
options: React.memo only works with class components
React.memo compares props deeply, so function props always look different
Any component that receives a function prop always re-renders whenever its parent renders
A new function is created every render, so the shallow check fails
questions.explanation: React.memo skips a re-render only when every prop is shallow-equal to the previous one; an inline arrow creates a new function reference each render, so memoize it with useCallback (with the right dependencies).

questions.question: In an Express app, req.body is undefined inside a POST /api/users handler even though the client sends JSON with Content-Type: application/json. What is the most likely cause?
options: The client must send the data as a query string instead of a body
The express.json() middleware is not registered, or is registered after the route
Express route handlers cannot read request bodies in POST routes
The route must be declared with app.get() instead of app.post() for req.body to be populated
questions.explanation: Express does not parse request bodies by default; app.use(express.json()) must be registered before the route so the JSON is parsed into req.body, because middleware runs in the order it is added.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to store user passwords in a database?
options: Hash them with a slow, salted algorithm like bcrypt
Encrypt them with AES so the server can decrypt and compare them during login
Store a single fast SHA-256 hash of each password
Encode them in Base64 so they are not human-readable
questions.explanation: Passwords should be hashed one-way with a deliberately slow, salted algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) so leaked hashes are expensive to crack; encryption is reversible and a fast unsalted SHA-256 is easy to brute-force.

questions.question: You are designing a MongoDB schema for a blog where a popular post can collect thousands of comments that are paginated and moderated on their own. Which design fits best?
options: Embed every comment in an array inside its post document
Add numbered fields such as comment1, comment2 to the post document
Keep comments in a separate database and merge them in the browser
Use a separate comments collection with an indexed postId field
questions.explanation: Unbounded arrays push documents toward MongoDB's 16 MB limit and are hard to paginate, so a separate comments collection referencing the post (with an index) scales better; embedding suits small, bounded data read together with its parent.

questions.question: Which Git command creates a new branch named feature-login and switches to it?
options: git branch feature-login --switch
git merge feature-login
git commit -b feature-login
git checkout -b feature-login
questions.explanation: git checkout -b <name> (or the newer git switch -c <name>) creates the branch and checks it out in one step; git branch <name> alone creates it without switching.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a .gitignore file?
options: It lists files and folders Git should not track, such as node_modules and .env
It deletes files from the remote repository
It hides selected commits from collaborators who do not have write access to the repository
It stores the credentials Git uses when pushing
questions.explanation: Patterns in .gitignore keep untracked files such as dependencies, build output and secrets out of commits; a file that is already tracked must first be removed with git rm --cached.

questions.question: Where should the production database password of a Node.js API be kept?
options: Hard-coded in the database connection file
In the React frontend bundle, so the browser can connect to the database directly
In an environment variable or a secrets manager
In the project README so new team members can find it
questions.explanation: Secrets belong in environment variables (e.g. process.env.DATABASE_URL) or the host's secrets manager so they stay out of source control and can differ per environment; anything in a frontend bundle is visible to every user.

questions.question: In Docker, what is the relationship between an image and a container?
options: An image is a running process; a container is the template it starts from
A container is a running instance created from an image
They are two names for exactly the same thing
An image is only for databases, while containers are for applications
questions.explanation: An image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile, and a container is a running (or stopped) instance of it; one image can start many containers.

questions.question: A team uses GitHub Actions for continuous integration. What should the workflow typically do when a pull request is opened?
options: Run install, lint, tests and a build to catch problems before merging
Merge the pull request into main as soon as it is opened
Delete the feature branch once a reviewer approves it
Squash and rewrite the branch history so that failing commits are hidden
questions.explanation: Continuous integration automatically builds and tests every change so broken code is caught before it reaches main; deployment (CD) usually runs after the merge.

questions.question: You pushed a commit that introduced a bug to the shared main branch, and teammates have already pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1, then git push --force to main
git commit --amend, then force-push main
git revert <commit-hash>, then push the new commit
Delete the remote main branch and push a fixed copy of it again
questions.explanation: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the bad one without rewriting shared history; reset or amend plus a force-push rewrites commits teammates already have and breaks their local branches.

questions.question: In a Node.js Dockerfile, why do teams copy package.json and package-lock.json and run npm ci before copying the rest of the source code?
options: So the dependency layer stays cached and is reused when only source code changes
Because npm ci fails when application source files are already present
So that node_modules is automatically left out of the final image
Because Docker always copies files in alphabetical order
questions.explanation: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a cached layer; if the package files have not changed, Docker reuses the npm ci layer and only re-copies the source, so rebuilds are much faster. Excluding node_modules is the job of .dockerignore.

questions.question: Your app authenticates users with a session cookie. Which cookie attribute most directly reduces the risk of cross-site request forgery (CSRF)?
options: HttpOnly
Secure
Max-Age=3600
SameSite=Lax
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax (or Strict) stops the browser from attaching the cookie to most requests started by other sites, which is what CSRF relies on; HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript (an XSS defence) and Secure only sends it over HTTPS.

questions.question: A build tool outputs files like main.3f9a1c.js whose names change whenever their content changes. Which response header is the best fit for serving these files?
options: Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Content-Type: text/html
questions.explanation: Because any content change produces a new filename, an old URL never needs revalidation, so browsers and CDNs can safely cache it for a year; no-store would force a full download on every visit.
